01001.description: Prattville is the seat of this central Alabama county, part of the Montgomery metropolitan area. The county has a humid subtropical climate.

01003.description: This county fronts the Gulf of Mexico and wraps around the eastern side of Mobile Bay, with the brackish Spanish River forming part of its western boundary. Bay Minette is the county seat; water makes up 21.6 percent of its area.

01005.description: The county spans southeastern Alabama’s Black Belt and Wiregrass regions. Eufaula is its largest city, while Clayton is the county seat.

01007.description: This central Alabama county sits within the Birmingham metropolitan area and is also included in the Appalachian Regional Commission’s definition of Appalachia. Centreville is its county seat.

01009.description: Oneonta is the county seat, and the area is known for three surviving covered bridges, including sites celebrated at an annual local festival. Those crossings are part of the county’s built landscape and local identity.

01011.description: Chunnenugga Ridge runs east to west across the county, dividing streams flowing toward the Tallapoosa River from waterways draining south toward the Gulf. Much of the terrain remains wooded, alongside cleared land used for farming or settlement.

01013.description: This south-central Alabama county lies in the Gulf Coastal Plain. Greenville is its county seat; the 2020 population was 19,051.

01015.description: Anniston is the county seat of this east-central Alabama county, part of the Anniston–Oxford metropolitan area. The 2020 population was 116,441.

01017.description: LaFayette is the county seat and Valley its largest city; the county is part of the LaGrange, Georgia–Alabama micropolitan area. This cross-state connection shapes its regional settlement context.

01019.description: Centre is the county seat of this northeastern Alabama county. Water covers about 7.7 percent of its area.

01021.description: The county’s landscape includes swamps, prairies, Appalachian foothills and the Coosa River. Clanton is the county seat, and the area is known for peach production.

01023.description: Butler is the county seat of this southwestern Alabama county. Its 2020 population was 12,665.

01025.description: Grove Hill is the county seat and Jackson the largest city of Clarke County in southwestern Alabama. It is the state’s third-largest county by land area and fourth-largest by total area.

01027.description: Ashland is the county seat of this east-central Alabama county. The 2020 population was 14,236.

01029.description: The county reaches Alabama’s eastern border with Georgia and contains Cheaha Mountain, the state’s highest natural point, within the southern Appalachian range. Heflin is the county seat.

01031.description: Elba is the county seat of this southeastern Alabama county, where Enterprise is the largest city. Both lie in the Wiregrass region; the 2020 population was 53,465.

01033.description: The county spans elevations from the Tennessee River valley in the northwest to higher ground in the southeast. Tuscumbia is the county seat, and the area belongs to the Florence–Muscle Shoals metropolitan area, commonly known as The Shoals.

01035.description: Evergreen is the county seat of this south-central Alabama county. The name Conecuh is believed to come from a Creek term meaning “land of cane.”

01037.description: The Coosa River forms part of the county’s boundary, and the county lies in Alabama’s Piedmont region. Rockford is its county seat, within the Talladega–Sylacauga micropolitan area.

01039.description: The county lies in the Gulf Coastal Plain and is drained by the Conecuh and Yellow rivers. Andalusia is the county seat, set within this south-central Alabama river landscape.

01041.description: South of the Montgomery metropolitan area, this Gulf Coastal Plain county includes extensive forested land used for logging. Luverne is its county seat.

01043.description: Cullman is both the county seat and largest city in this north-central Alabama county. Its metropolitan area is linked to the wider Birmingham–Hoover–Talladega region.

01045.description: The Wiregrass region frames this southeastern Alabama county, where Ozark serves as both county seat and largest city. Most of Fort Rucker, now named Fort Novosel, is also located here.

01047.description: Selma is the county seat and center of this central Alabama micropolitan area. Its 2020 population was 38,462.

01049.description: Fort Payne is the county seat in this northeastern Alabama county, part of the Huntsville–Decatur–Albertville combined statistical area. Water covers 0.2 percent of its area.

01051.description: The county sits along Alabama’s fall line, where rolling Piedmont terrain and river cities such as Wetumpka and Tallassee meet. Farmland and open fields occur alongside this varied landscape; manufacturing is identified as its largest employment sector.

01053.description: This south-central county includes the Poarch Band of Creek Indians, Alabama’s only federally recognized tribe, based here. Brewton is the county seat, and the county forms the Atmore micropolitan area within the broader Pensacola region.

01055.description: Gadsden is the county seat of this northeastern Alabama county, which is the state’s smallest by total area. The 2020 population was 103,436, making it a comparatively concentrated settlement area.

01057.description: Fayette is both the county seat and largest city of this Alabama county. The 2020 population was 16,321.

01059.description: Russellville is the county seat of this northwestern Alabama county. The 2020 population was 32,113.

01061.description: Geneva is the county seat of this southern Alabama county. The 2020 population was 26,659.

01063.description: The Tombigbee and Black Warrior river systems shape much of this west-central county’s boundary. Eutaw is the county seat; the 2020 population was 7,730, the smallest among Alabama counties in that census.

01065.description: Greensboro is the county seat of this west-central Alabama county, part of the Tuscaloosa metropolitan area. Water covers about 1.9 percent of its area.

01067.description: This southeastern county lies in the Wiregrass region and is part of the Dothan metropolitan area. Abbeville is its county seat, set within a region of smaller settlements.

01069.description: At Alabama’s southeastern corner, this county is part of the Dothan metropolitan area. Its seat is Dothan, a city that also extends across the border into neighboring Henry County.

01071.description: This northeastern Alabama county lies largely in the Appalachians and includes Russell Cave National Monument, an archaeological site with evidence of thousands of years of human occupation. Scottsboro is the county seat and the center of the county’s micropolitan area.

01073.description: Birmingham anchors this county as its largest city and county seat, within the state’s most prominent urban center. The county’s 2020 population was 674,721, reflecting its large metropolitan settlement base.

01075.description: Vernon is the county seat of this northwestern Alabama county. Its 2020 population was 13,972.

01077.description: The Tennessee River forms the southern and western boundaries of this northwestern Alabama county. Florence is the county seat, and the county is part of the Florence–Muscle Shoals metropolitan area.

01079.description: Moulton is the county seat of this northern Alabama county, which is part of the Decatur metropolitan area. The 2020 population was 33,073.

01081.description: This east-central Alabama county straddles the fall line, with hillier Piedmont terrain to the north and flatter Gulf Coastal Plain to the south. Opelika is the county seat and Auburn its largest city.

01083.description: Athens is the county seat of this northern Alabama county. The 2020 population was 103,570.

01085.description: Hayneville is the county seat of this central Alabama county, south of Montgomery. The 2020 population was 10,311.

01087.description: Tuskegee is the county seat of this east-central Alabama county in the Black Belt. Its economy developed around cotton agriculture; the 2020 population was 19,532.

01089.description: Huntsville is the county seat and center of this county’s metropolitan area. Since the mid-20th century, defense and space research and industry have become important economic sectors.

01091.description: The Tombigbee River forms the entire western boundary, with a small section of the Black Warrior River along the northwest. Linden is the county seat, while Demopolis is the largest city.

01093.description: Hamilton is the county seat of this northwestern Alabama county, which borders Mississippi and covers 743 square miles.

01095.description: The Tennessee River runs both north and south within the county, and Guntersville is its county seat. The Albertville micropolitan area connects it to the wider Huntsville–Decatur region.

01097.description: Mobile is the county seat and Alabama’s principal deepwater port, linking the county to the Mobile River, inland waterways and the Gulf of Mexico. The county also includes several islands, including Dauphin Island, and about a quarter of its area is water.

01099.description: Monroeville is the county seat in this southwestern Alabama county. Its local literary associations include Harper Lee’s long residence and Truman Capote’s childhood home, both tied to the town’s setting.

01101.description: Montgomery, Alabama’s state capital, is also the county seat and the center of the county’s metropolitan area. The county’s 2020 population was 228,954.

01103.description: Decatur is the county seat of this north-central Alabama county, part of the Decatur metropolitan area. The county belongs to the wider Huntsville–Decatur–Albertville combined statistical area.

01105.description: The southern half of this county lies in the Gulf Coastal Plain, while its northern half reaches the southern Ridge-and-Valley Appalachian foothills. Marion is the county seat; the landscape includes forested hills and valleys.

01107.description: This west-central county lies between Tuscaloosa County and the Mississippi border. Carrollton is its county seat, within the broader Tuscaloosa metropolitan area.

01109.description: Troy is the county seat and center of this county’s micropolitan area. The 2020 population was 33,009.

01111.description: Wedowee is the county seat of this central-eastern Alabama county. The 2020 population was 21,967.

01113.description: Phenix City is the county seat of this easternmost Alabama county, part of the Columbus, Georgia–Alabama metropolitan area. More than half of its residents work across the state line, mostly in Columbus.

01115.description: This county has two seats, Ashville and Pell City, an unusual arrangement in Alabama. It is part of the Birmingham metropolitan area.

01117.description: The county combines the southern extensions of the Appalachians, flatter farm and pasture land, and lowlands along the Cahaba and Coosa rivers. Lay Lake also borders it, while Columbiana is the county seat and Alabaster its largest city.

01119.description: The Noxubee River crosses this Black Belt county in west-central Alabama. Livingston is the county seat and home to the University of West Alabama.

01121.description: Located in the Coosa River Valley and Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians, the county includes Mount Cheaha along its northeastern border. Talladega is the county seat, and streams including Choccolocco Creek drain the area.

01123.description: This county lies in Alabama’s Piedmont region, with water covering about 6.5 percent of its area. Dadeville is the county seat and Alexander City its largest settlement.

01125.description: This county straddles the Appalachian Highlands and Gulf Coastal Plain, creating a varied landscape that includes part of Talladega National Forest. Tuscaloosa is its county seat and the region’s main center for education, industry and health care.

01127.description: Jasper is the county seat of this Cumberland Plateau county, whose terrain includes forested plateaus and valleys. Coal mining is described by local officials as central to the county economy.

01129.description: The Tombigbee River borders this southwestern county, whose land is 88 percent forest and pine plantations. Chatom is the county seat, roughly 60 miles north of the Gulf of Mexico.

01131.description: Camden is the county seat of this Alabama county. Major industrial employers include a paper mill near Pine Hill and a copper tubing plant in Sunny South.

01133.description: Double Springs is the county seat of this northwestern Alabama county. Its 2020 population was 23,540.

02013.description: The borough spans the western Alaska Peninsula and scattered islands, including the Shumagin, Pavlof and Sanak groups; water accounts for about 53.5 percent of its area. Commercial fishing and fish processing anchor the economy, with Sand Point home to the Aleutian Chain’s largest fishing fleet.

02016.description: This census area extends across most of the Aleutian Islands from Attu to Unalaska, as well as the Pribilof Islands in the Bering Sea. Unalaska is its largest city and home to about 80 percent of the population; the area has no borough seat.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Aleutians West Census Area, Alaska

02020.description: Anchorage occupies a coastal plain at the head of Cook Inlet, between Knik Arm and Turnagain Arm, with the Chugach Mountains rising along its eastern edge. Its economy includes transportation, government, military activity, tourism and resource extraction.

02050.description: The census area includes Nunivak Island in the Bering Sea and has no borough seat because it lies in Alaska’s unorganized borough. Bethel is its largest community; the 2020 population was 18,666.

02060.description: This small borough occupies a coastal stretch around Naknek and inland King Salmon on Bristol Bay. Naknek is the borough seat, and the 2020 population was 844; the borough has no incorporated settlements.

02068.description: Denali, North America’s highest point, lies within this borough, where Healy is the seat and largest community. Tourism around Denali National Park, the Usibelli coal mine and Clear Space Force Station contribute to local development.

02070.description: Dillingham, the largest community, sits on a small arm of Bristol Bay along the Bering Sea. This unorganized census area had 4,857 residents in 2020 and has no borough seat.

02090.description: Fairbanks is the seat of this borough, which includes the University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fort Wainwright and Eielson Air Force Base. The 2020 population was 95,655, and it forms one of Alaska’s two metropolitan areas.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fairbanks North Star Borough, Alaska

02100.description: Haines Borough had 2,080 residents in the 2020 census. It is a home-rule borough in Southeast Alaska.

02105.description: This census area in Southeast Alaska had 2,365 residents in 2020 and has no borough seat. Hoonah is its largest community; water makes up 31.1 percent of the area.

02110.description: Juneau lies along Gastineau Channel, with downtown below Mount Juneau and Douglas Island across the water. Government is a major employer, while tourism brings most of its income during the summer cruise season.

02122.description: The borough includes most of the Kenai Peninsula and a large mainland area across Cook Inlet. Soldotna is the borough seat, Kenai the largest city, and Kalifornsky its most populous community.

02130.description: Ketchikan is the borough seat and center of this Southeast Alaska micropolitan area. Water makes up 27.0 percent of its area, which expanded in 2008 to include much of the former Prince of Wales–Outer Ketchikan census area.

02150.description: The borough includes Kodiak Island and numerous neighboring islands, as well as a narrow mainland strip across Shelikof Strait. Water makes up about 45.5 percent of its area, and Kodiak is the borough seat.

02164.description: This borough covers much of the Alaska Peninsula and contains Iliamna Lake, the largest lake in Alaska. Port Alsworth is its most populous community, while the borough seat, King Salmon, is located in neighboring Bristol Bay Borough.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Lake and Peninsula Borough, Alaska

02170.description: The Matanuska and Susitna rivers flow south into Cook Inlet across this borough, one of Alaska’s few agricultural areas. Palmer is the seat and Wasilla the largest incorporated community; its 2020 population was 107,081.

02180.description: Nome is the largest community in this unorganized census area, which lies along the Bering Sea coast. The 2020 population was 10,046, and the area has no borough seat.

02185.description: Utqiaġvik is the seat and largest city of North Slope Borough, the northernmost county equivalent in the United States. Its western coastline borders the Chukchi Sea and its eastern shores the Beaufort Sea.

02188.description: This borough lies along the Chukchi Sea coast in northwestern Alaska, with Kotzebue as its seat and largest community. The borough had 7,793 residents in the 2020 census; Kotzebue Sound is an important wildlife area.

02195.description: Petersburg Borough had 3,398 residents in 2020. Petersburg is the borough seat and primary community in this Southeast Alaska coastal area.

02198.description: This census area includes Prince of Wales Island, the Hyder area and Annette Island. Metlakatla and Craig are its largest communities; it has no borough seat and had 5,753 residents in 2020.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Prince of Wales–Hyder Census Area, Alaska

02220.description: Sitka’s borough combines a coastal community with extensive island and mainland territory in Southeast Alaska. Its population was 8,458 in 2020.

02230.description: Skagway Borough is centered on the community of Skagway in Southeast Alaska. Its population was 1,240 in the 2020 census.

02240.description: This census area in Alaska’s Interior had 6,808 residents in 2020. It is part of the unorganized borough and has no borough seat; Deltana and Tok are its largest communities.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Southeast Fairbanks Census Area, Alaska

02275.description: The borough of Wrangell had 2,127 residents in 2020. It is centered on a coastal community in Southeast Alaska.

02282.description: Yakutat Borough is a remote coastal area on the Gulf of Alaska, where Hubbard Glacier, North America’s largest tidewater glacier, meets Russell Fjord. Its 2020 population was 657.

02290.description: This extensive unorganized census area is larger than Montana, with Galena and Fort Yukon as its largest communities. Its 2020 population was 5,343, spread across small communities in Alaska’s Interior.

04001.description: The county spans northeastern Arizona and includes portions of the Navajo Nation and Fort Apache and Zuni reservations. St. Johns is the county seat; the 2020 population was 66,021.

04003.description: Bisbee is the county seat and Sierra Vista the most populous city in Cochise County. The county occupies Arizona’s southeastern corner and borders New Mexico and the Mexican state of Sonora.

04005.description: Coconino County contains the Grand Canyon, the state’s highest natural point at Humphreys Peak, and Barringer Meteor Crater. Flagstaff is the county seat, while tourism, Northern Arizona University and other major institutions shape the local economy.

04007.description: This central Arizona county includes parts of the Fort Apache and San Carlos Apache reservations. Globe is the county seat, and the Payson micropolitan area links it to the wider Phoenix region.

04009.description: Mount Graham rises within the Pinaleño Mountains in this southeastern Arizona county. Safford is the county seat and anchor of its micropolitan area; the county also contains Eastern Arizona College and Mount Graham International Observatory.

04011.description: The county is Arizona’s least populous and second-smallest by area, with Clifton as its seat. The Morenci copper mine dominates its economy, accounting for about 90 percent of county GDP and 70 percent of jobs in 2024.

04012.description: The Colorado River borders this western Arizona county, whose seat is Parker. Its name comes from the early riverside settlement of La Paz; the county had 16,557 residents in 2020.

04013.description: Phoenix, Arizona’s capital, is the county seat and center of the Phoenix–Mesa–Chandler metropolitan area. The county includes five tribal communities and held about 62 percent of the state’s population in the 2020 census.

04015.description: The county is split into two sections by the Grand Canyon, with no direct land connection between them. Its western boundary follows the Colorado River in the south; Kingman is the seat, and the county includes parts of Grand Canyon and Lake Mead protected areas.

04017.description: This northern Arizona county includes parts of the Hopi and Navajo nations and Fort Apache Indian Reservation. Its landscapes range from Monument Valley and Petrified Forest National Park to extensive ponderosa pine forest; Holbrook is the county seat.

04019.description: Tucson anchors this south-central Arizona county, which also includes portions of the Tohono O’odham Nation and several protected areas. Saguaro National Park and Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument are among its distinctive landscapes.

04021.description: Pinal County lies between Phoenix and Tucson, with suburban growth extending inward from both metropolitan areas. Florence is the county seat; the county also includes the Ak-Chin Indian Community and portions of several other tribal lands.

04023.description: Nogales sits on the county’s southern border with Sonora, Mexico, and serves as the county seat. Santa Cruz is Arizona’s smallest county by area and part of the Tucson–Nogales combined region.

04025.description: Yavapai County’s topography rises from the Sonoran Desert to the Coconino Plateau and Mogollon Rim. Prescott is the county seat; the county also includes northern portions of Peoria and Wickenburg in the Phoenix metropolitan area.

04027.description: The county lies in the Sonoran Desert at Arizona’s southwestern corner, where the Colorado River reaches its lowest point in the state. Yuma is the county seat; winter vegetable production makes it Arizona’s leading agricultural county by value.

05001.description: This Arkansas Delta county lies on the Mississippi Alluvial Plain, where flat, fertile deposits define the Grand Prairie. It has two county seats, DeWitt and Stuttgart, and the landscape’s broad agricultural plain is a defining local feature.

05003.description: Bayou Bartholomew divides this South Arkansas county between the fertile alluvial soils of the Mississippi Plain and other terrain to the west. Timber and agriculture have long shaped the local economy; Hamburg is the seat and Crossett the largest city.

05005.description: Baxter County sits on the Salem Plateau in the Ozarks, where steep, rocky ground and oak–hickory–pine forest surround Bull Shoals Lake, Norfork Lake and the White River. Mountain Home is the seat and largest city.

05007.description: This northwest Arkansas county lies on the Springfield Plateau of the Ozarks, with gently rolling ground and karst features such as caves, springs and sinkholes. Bentonville is the county seat, and Rogers is its most populous city.

05009.description: Rolling Springfield and Salem plateaus cover much of this Ozark county along the Missouri border, while the more rugged Boston Mountains lie to the south. Harrison is the county seat and the center of its micropolitan area.

05011.description: The Saline River valley marks the southeastern edge of Bradley County, where the Mississippi Embayment extends inland. Warren is the county seat; the 2020 population was 10,545.

05013.description: Hampton is the county seat of Arkansas’s least populous county, with 4,739 residents in the 2020 census. It forms part of the Camden micropolitan area in south-central Arkansas.

05015.description: Carroll County has two county seats, Berryville and Eureka Springs. The county’s population was 28,260 in the 2020 census.

05017.description: Lake Village, the county seat, sits in the southeastern corner of Arkansas within the Delta lowlands along the Mississippi River. Water covers about 6.7 percent of the county, which had 10,208 residents in 2020.

05019.description: Arkadelphia is the county seat and center of this south-central Arkansas micropolitan area. Its 2020 population was 21,446.

05021.description: The county lies largely on the flat Mississippi Alluvial Plain, where rice is the dominant crop alongside cotton, soybeans, corn, hay and milo. Corning and Piggott share the county seat, with factories in both towns and in Rector.

05023.description: Greers Ferry Lake accounts for much of the county’s water area, extending west into neighboring Van Buren County. Heber Springs is both the county seat and largest city.

05025.description: Rison is the county seat and largest city of this county, which is part of the Little Rock metropolitan area. Its 2020 population was 7,550.

05027.description: Dorcheat Bayou flows south through this South Arkansas county toward Louisiana, and the area shares the country’s largest bromine reserve with neighboring Union County. Magnolia is the seat and home to Southern Arkansas University.

05029.description: This county occupies a low, fertile stretch of the Arkansas River Valley between the Ozarks and Ouachita Mountains. Morrilton is the county seat and largest city, northwest of Little Rock.

05031.description: Crowley’s Ridge is the most prominent landform in this northeastern Arkansas county. Jonesboro and Lake City share the county seat, and the 2020 population was 111,231.

05033.description: Most of this northwestern county lies in the Ozarks, with Van Buren as its county seat and largest city. Water covers about 1.8 percent of its area.

05035.description: Marion is the county seat and West Memphis the largest city in this Arkansas county, part of the Memphis metropolitan area. The county’s 2020 population was 48,163.

05037.description: The county lies on fertile alluvial soils of the Mississippi Plain, bisected north to south by Crowley’s Ridge, a loess formation that remains generally forested. Wynne is its county seat and largest city amid a landscape otherwise used extensively for row crops.

05039.description: Fordyce is the county seat of this south-central Arkansas county, whose 2020 population was 6,482. It ranked among the state’s least populous counties in that census.

05041.description: This Delta county borders the Mississippi River along its eastern edge, and water covers about 6.3 percent of its area. Arkansas City is the county seat; the 2020 population was 11,395.

05043.description: Most of Drew County is in the Piney Woods of the South Central Plains, with its eastern edge along Bayou Bartholomew in the Delta. Monticello is the county seat and largest city, serving as a regional center.

05045.description: Conway, the county seat and largest city, anchors this Central Arkansas county. The 2020 population was 123,498, the fifth-largest among Arkansas counties.

05047.description: Franklin County has two county seats, Charleston and Ozark. The 2020 population was 17,097.

05049.description: Salem is the county seat of this north-central Arkansas county, which had 12,075 residents in the 2020 census.

05051.description: Hot Springs National Park lies within Garland County, whose county seat is Hot Springs. Water covers about 7.7 percent of the county, which forms its own metropolitan area.

05053.description: Sheridan is the county seat of Grant County in the Arkansas Timberlands. The county is part of the Little Rock–North Little Rock–Conway metropolitan area and had 17,958 residents in 2020.

05055.description: Paragould, the county seat, sits atop Crowley’s Ridge in this northeastern Arkansas county. The county is part of the Jonesboro–Paragould combined statistical area.

05057.description: Hope is the county seat of this southwestern Arkansas county, part of the broader South Arkansas region. Its population was 20,065 in 2020, down from 22,609 in 2010.

05059.description: This Southwest Arkansas county lies largely in the forested, mountainous Ouachitas, with deep valleys and the Ouachita River crossing the region. Malvern is the county seat.

05061.description: Nashville is the county seat of this southwestern Arkansas county, which had 12,785 residents in the 2020 census.

05063.description: Batesville is the county seat and center of this north-central Arkansas micropolitan area. The county had 37,938 residents in the 2020 census.

05065.description: Melbourne is the county seat of this Arkansas county, which had 13,577 residents in the 2020 census.

05067.description: Newport is both the largest city and county seat in this Arkansas Delta county. The county contains seven incorporated towns and four cities, with settlements spread across the Mississippi Alluvial Plain.

05069.description: The Arkansas River bisects this Delta county and has long served as its main transportation route. Pine Bluff is the county seat; the 2020 census counted 67,260 residents.

05071.description: Clarksville is the county seat of this Arkansas county. The 2020 census counted 25,749 residents.

05073.description: Lafayette County is Arkansas’s smallest county by area, with Lewisville as its seat. Agriculture, livestock and poultry, pine logging and oil production are established activities, while lithium brines in the Smackover formation have prompted early commercial development.

05075.description: Walnut Ridge is the county seat of this northeastern Arkansas county, which had 16,216 residents in the 2020 census.

05077.description: The Mississippi River forms the eastern boundary of this Delta county, where Marianna is the county seat. The county had 8,600 residents in 2020.

05079.description: Bayou Bartholomew divides this county between forested Arkansas Timberlands to the west and the Delta to the east. Star City is the county seat, and state correctional facilities are among the area’s major employers.

05081.description: This county sits in Arkansas’s southwest corner, where the borders of Texas and Oklahoma meet. Ashdown is the county seat, and the county is part of the Texarkana metropolitan area.

05083.description: Magazine Mountain, Arkansas’s highest natural point, lies within Logan County. Booneville and Paris share the county seat, and the area had 21,131 residents in 2020.

05085.description: Lonoke County lies in the Central Arkansas metropolitan area, with Lonoke as its seat and Cabot its largest city. The county’s 2020 population was 74,015.

05087.description: Huntsville is the county seat of Madison County in the Northwest Arkansas region. Its population was 16,521 in the 2020 census.

05089.description: Yellville is the county seat of this Ozark county, which includes four incorporated cities and one incorporated town. Water makes up about 6.8 percent of its area.

05091.description: Pine forests and cleared fields characterize this southwestern county, where rice, soybeans, corn and vegetables are grown. Texarkana is the county seat, and the county is part of the cross-state Ark-La-Tex region.

05093.description: The Mississippi River borders this easternmost Arkansas county, where Blytheville and Osceola share the county seat. Its economy shifted from agriculture toward steel manufacturing beginning in the 1980s, with major plants and infrastructure investments.

05095.description: Monroe County lies on the flat, fertile Mississippi Alluvial Plain, including part of the Grand Prairie. Clarendon is the county seat and Brinkley the largest city.

05097.description: Mount Ida is the county seat of this Ouachita Mountains county in western Arkansas. The 2020 population was 8,484.

05099.description: The Little Missouri River bounds this southwestern county to the north, and tributaries drain toward the Ouachita and Red rivers. Prescott is the county seat; the 2020 census counted 8,310 residents.

05101.description: This Ozark county lies almost entirely in the rugged Boston Mountains, where the Buffalo National River is a major recreation destination. Jasper is the county seat, and the county is part of the Harrison micropolitan area.

05103.description: The Ouachita River gives this south-central county its name. Camden is the county seat and center of the local micropolitan area.

05105.description: Perry County is among Arkansas’s smallest counties by area, with Perryville as its county seat. The county had 10,019 residents in 2020 and is part of the Little Rock metropolitan region.

05107.description: This eastern Arkansas Delta county lies along the Mississippi River, with Helena–West Helena as its county seat. The river-adjacent county had 16,568 residents in 2020.

05109.description: Murfreesboro is the county seat of this southwestern Arkansas county, which had 10,171 residents in the 2020 census.

05111.description: Crowley’s Ridge and the L’Anguille River run north to south through this northeastern county. Eastern soils deposited by the Mississippi River are used mainly for cotton farming; Harrisburg is the county seat.

05113.description: Mena is the county seat of this Arkansas county, which had 19,221 residents in the 2020 census.

05115.description: Russellville is the county seat of this Arkansas county, whose 2020 census population was 63,381.

05117.description: The county contains part of the Grand Prairie, a Delta subregion associated with rice cultivation and aquaculture. It has two county seats, DeValls Bluff and Des Arc, and agriculture is its largest employment sector.

05119.description: Little Rock, Arkansas’s capital and largest city, is the county seat and the core of the state’s largest metropolitan area. Pulaski County had 399,125 residents in 2020, the largest population of any Arkansas county.

05121.description: This county meets where Ozark foothills give way to the Arkansas Delta, bringing upland and alluvial landscapes together. Pocahontas is the county seat; local employers include food processing and schools.

05123.description: Forrest City is the county seat of this east-central Arkansas county, part of the Memphis–Forrest City regional area. Its 2020 population was 23,090.

05125.description: Benton is both the county seat and largest city in this Central Arkansas county. The name Saline refers to the area’s brine springs; the county had 123,416 residents in 2020.

05127.description: Waldron is the county seat of this western Arkansas county. The 2020 census counted 9,836 residents.

05129.description: Marshall is the county seat of this north-central Arkansas county. The 2020 census counted 7,828 residents.

05131.description: Sebastian County has two county seats, Greenwood and Fort Smith, and is part of the Fort Smith metropolitan area. It is among Arkansas’s smallest counties by area despite a 2020 population of 127,799.

05133.description: This southwestern county’s landscape includes five lakes, several rivers and mountain streams, and forests. De Queen is the county seat; the local “Land of Lakes” description reflects its many inland waters.

05135.description: Ash Flat is the county seat of this north-central Arkansas county. Its 2020 census population was 17,271.

05137.description: The county contains parts of three Ozark subregions: the Springfield and Salem plateaus and the steeper Boston Mountains. Mountain View is both the county seat and largest city.

05139.description: Union County is Arkansas’s largest county by area and shares the country’s largest bromine reserve with Columbia County. El Dorado is the county seat; the Ouachita River marks the state’s lowest point within the county.

05141.description: Clinton is the county seat of this north-central Arkansas county, with water making up about 2.2 percent of its area. The 2020 population was 15,796.

05143.description: Fayetteville and Springdale are among the 13 incorporated municipalities in this Northwest Arkansas county. The Ozark landscape shifts from the grassy Springfield Plateau toward the lower Boston Mountains; Fayetteville is the county seat.

05145.description: Searcy is the county seat of this central Arkansas county, the state’s second-largest by area. Its 2020 population was 76,822; local institutions include a regional bank and a Walmart distribution center.

05147.description: This county lies in the Arkansas Delta, a flat expanse of Mississippi River sediments. Augusta is the county seat, and the Cache River runs through the county’s agricultural landscape.

05149.description: Yell County has two county seats, Dardanelle and Danville. The 2020 census counted 20,263 residents.

06001.description: Alameda County occupies much of the East Bay, with the San Francisco Bay on its western edge and the Berkeley Hills along part of its border. Oakland is the county seat; its 2020 population was 1,682,353.

06003.description: This eastern Sierra Nevada county borders Nevada, and about 96 percent of its land is federally owned, including portions of three national forests. Markleeville is the county seat; Alpine was California’s least populous county in 2020.

06005.description: Jackson is the county seat of Amador County in California’s Sierra Nevada and Gold Country. The county has a substantial wine industry, including old Zinfandel vineyards, and water bodies such as Lake Amador and the Mokelumne River.

06007.description: The Feather River drains this county on the western slope of the Sierra Nevada, where steep terrain supports several hydroelectric plants. Oroville is the county seat, and Chico is the center of the county’s metropolitan area.

06009.description: Caverns and Sierra foothill terrain distinguish this Gold Country county, where San Andreas is the seat and Angels Camp the only incorporated city. Vineyards and wineries remain part of the local economy.

06011.description: This northern Sacramento Valley county is drained by several creeks, and the Sacramento River forms part of its eastern boundary. Colusa is the county seat.

06013.description: The county’s terrain ranges from a bayside alluvial plain and inland valleys to the Oakland–Berkeley hills and Mount Diablo. Martinez is the county seat of this largely suburban part of the East Bay.

06015.description: At California’s far northwest corner, the county meets the Pacific and Oregon border. Its Klamath and Coast Range mountains descend to small coastal flats and isolated valleys; Crescent City is the county seat and only incorporated city.

06017.description: This Sierra Nevada county spans the Gold Country foothills and part of the Lake Tahoe Basin. Placerville is the county seat; the 2020 population was 191,185.

06019.description: Fresno County occupies the Central Valley, where agriculture is a leading industry and the county is a major producer of pistachios and cotton. Fresno is the county seat and the hub of its metropolitan area.

06021.description: Willows is the county seat of this northern Sacramento Valley county. The Grindstone Indian Rancheria of Wintun-Wailaki Indians is located within its boundaries.

06023.description: Humboldt Bay, a deepwater port on the North Coast, sits near the midpoint of this county’s coastline. Eureka is the county seat; redwood timber, dairy production and orchards in warmer inland valleys are among the area’s economic activities.

06025.description: Much of this southeastern county lies below sea level, yet irrigation has made its desert soils highly productive farmland. Agriculture is the largest industry, and El Centro is the county seat and largest city.

06027.description: Inyo County stretches between the Sierra Nevada and Nevada, from Mount Whitney on its western border to Badwater Basin in Death Valley. Independence is the county seat; the two extremes are among the highest and lowest points in the contiguous United States.

06029.description: Kern County spans the southern Central Valley, the Coast Range slopes and the southern Sierra Nevada. Bakersfield is the county seat; agriculture, oil and gas, and renewable energy production are major industries.

06031.description: Kings County lies in the agricultural San Joaquin Valley, where about 87 percent of its land is farmland. Hanford is the county seat, and milk is its leading agricultural commodity by value.

06033.description: Clear Lake dominates this north-central county and drains via Cache Creek toward the Sacramento River. Lakeport is the county seat; healthcare, tribal casinos and geothermal energy are among its major employers.

06035.description: Susanville is both the county seat and largest city of this northeastern California county. Its economy now relies heavily on federal and state prison employment; a corner of Lassen Volcanic National Park extends into the county.

06037.description: Los Angeles County encompasses 88 cities and 101 unincorporated communities in Southern California. Its 2025 population estimate was 9,694,934, and entertainment, digital media and international trade are among its major industries.

06039.description: This county spans the eastern San Joaquin Valley, Sierra foothills and central Sierra Nevada, with part of Yosemite National Park inside its boundaries. Madera is the county seat; agriculture is a major sector, led by almonds, grapes and pistachios.

06041.description: Across the Golden Gate from San Francisco, Marin County includes coast, bays and inland ranges; water makes up 37.2 percent of its area. San Rafael is both county seat and largest city.

06043.description: The eastern portion of this Sierra Nevada county contains much of Yosemite National Park. Mariposa is the county seat, and tourism is the dominant industry; visitors spent $433.2 million in the county in 2023, according to the local tourism bureau.

06045.description: Ukiah is the county seat of this North Coast county, which forms its own micropolitan area. The Pacific-facing county had 91,601 residents in the 2020 census.

06047.description: Merced County sits in the northern San Joaquin Valley and is named for the Merced River. Merced is the county seat, and the county produces about 90 percent of California’s sweet potato crop.

06049.description: This northeastern California county borders Nevada and Oregon, with much of its land federally owned. Alturas is its county seat and only incorporated city; the 2020 population was 8,700.

06051.description: Mono County sits east of the Sierra Nevada between Yosemite and Nevada, with Bridgeport as the county seat and Mammoth Lakes as its only incorporated town. White Mountain Peak, California’s third-highest summit, rises within the county.

06053.description: Monterey County’s Pacific coast includes the southern half of Monterey Bay, while Salinas anchors its inland valley. The county seat is also its largest city; the county had 439,035 residents in 2020.

06055.description: Napa Valley’s rolling hills support wine grapes, but oak woodland covers roughly a third of the county, alongside chaparral and other landscapes. Napa is the county seat; the 2020 population was 138,019.

sources.title: Napa County watershed information: Oak woodlands

06057.description: The Middle and South Yuba rivers drain this Sierra Nevada county, part of California’s Gold Country. Nevada City is the county seat, and the county forms the Truckee–Grass Valley micropolitan area.

06059.description: This mostly suburban county in Greater Los Angeles had 3,186,989 residents in the 2020 census. It is bordered by the Pacific Ocean and is the smallest county by area in Southern California.

06061.description: Placer County extends from the Sacramento Valley across the Sierra Nevada to Lake Tahoe, whose surface area is partly within the county. Auburn is the county seat, and the 2020 population was 404,739.

06063.description: The county occupies the northern Sierra Nevada, where rugged terrain marks a transition toward the Cascade Range. Quincy is the county seat, and the Feather River flows through the area.

06065.description: Riverside County is part of the Inland Empire and spans a broad east–west stretch of Southern California. Its 2020 population was 2,418,185, and its land area is roughly comparable to New Jersey.

06067.description: Sacramento, California’s capital, is the county seat and center of the Greater Sacramento metropolitan area. Much of the county lies near sea level, with several major rivers including the Sacramento and American.

06069.description: The San Benito River crosses almost the full length of this Central Coast county before joining the Pajaro River. Hollister is the county seat; agriculture remains the dominant activity alongside wineries and farm visits.

06071.description: San Bernardino County is California’s largest by area, extending across the Inland Empire to the borders of Nevada and Arizona. The 2020 population was 2,181,654, with most residents concentrated in its southern portion.

06073.description: San Diego County reaches from the Pacific coast to the Mexican border in Southern California. San Diego is the county seat and a major urban center; the 2020 population was 3,298,634.

06075.description: San Francisco is a city and county at the northern end of the San Francisco Peninsula, with shoreline on both the Pacific Ocean and San Francisco Bay. Its service economy includes tourism, finance and technology.

06077.description: This low, flat San Joaquin Valley county contains a marshy delta drained by the San Joaquin River and its tributaries. Stockton is the county seat; agriculture generated $2.6 billion in gross value in 2018.

06079.description: This Central Coast county reaches from the Pacific across the Santa Lucia Range, with the Salinas River draining Paso Robles and San Luis Obispo Creek flowing through the county seat. Strawberries and wine grapes led agricultural crop value in 2024.

sources.title: Wikipedia: San Luis Obispo County, California

06081.description: San Mateo County occupies the peninsula between San Francisco Bay and the Pacific, with about 40 percent of its area covered by water. Redwood City is the county seat; the area is also part of Silicon Valley.

06083.description: The county spans Southern California’s coast and rugged backcountry, with Santa Barbara as its seat and Santa Maria its largest city. Oil fields in the Santa Maria Valley and elsewhere have supplied oil, gas and asphalt for decades.

06085.description: San Jose anchors Santa Clara County, the South Bay center of the San Francisco Bay Area. Technology, including hardware and software, dominates the services-based economy; the 2020 population was 1,936,000.

06087.description: This Pacific coastal county lies between broad beaches and the crest of the Santa Cruz Mountains. Tourism has become a major economic sector; Santa Cruz is the county seat and center of its metropolitan area.

06089.description: Mountains line this northern California county on three sides, while the Sacramento River flows south through its center toward the Sacramento Valley. Redding is the county seat and center of its metropolitan area.

06091.description: This county occupies the Sierra Nevada along the Nevada border, with landscapes ranging from forests and mountains to lakes and streams. Downieville is the county seat, and Loyalton its only incorporated city.

06093.description: Mount Shasta rises near the center of this large county along the Oregon border, amid a mix of forests, lakes, desert and chaparral. Yreka is the county seat; outdoor recreation and tourism are important destinations.

06095.description: Fairfield is the county seat of this northeastern San Francisco Bay Area county, part of the Vallejo–Fairfield metropolitan area. Water covers about 9.3 percent of its area.

06097.description: Sonoma County’s North Coast ranges include the Mayacamas and Sonoma Mountains, with vineyards across the region. Agriculture remains a key part of the local economy; Santa Rosa is the county seat and largest city.

06099.description: The San Joaquin River historically divided this valley county’s communities and trade routes. Modesto is the county seat, and agriculture—especially almonds—is the county’s leading industry.

06101.description: About 88 percent of this Sacramento Valley county is prime farmland and grazing land. The Sutter Buttes rise above the otherwise flat valley; Yuba City is the county seat.

06103.description: The Sacramento River bisects this northern California county, and a corner of Lassen Volcanic National Park extends into its northeast. Red Bluff is both county seat and largest city.

06105.description: Weaverville is the county seat of this rugged, mountainous and heavily forested county, where the Trinity River runs through its terrain. The county contains a significant portion of Shasta–Trinity National Forest and the Trinity Alps Wilderness.

06107.description: Tulare County’s economy is led by dairy, with milk products typically generating over $1 billion annually. Visalia is the county seat; the county’s namesake lake was drained for agriculture and now lies in Kings County.

06109.description: Tuolumne County lies in the Sierra Nevada, and the northern half of Yosemite National Park is within its eastern portion. Sonora is both the county seat and only incorporated city.

06111.description: The county includes the Oxnard Plain and valleys of the Transverse Ranges, with about 53 percent of its area in national forest. Ventura is the county seat, while Oxnard is the largest city; lemons are a major crop.

06113.description: Woodland is the county seat of this northern Sacramento Valley county, which is part of the greater Sacramento metropolitan area. The 2020 population was 216,403.

06115.description: The county follows the Feather River along the western slope of the Sierra Nevada, with most residents on the valley floor around Marysville. Steep mountain slopes support hydroelectric power generation.

08001.description: This Denver-area county surrounds much of Denver International Airport, with Brighton as its seat and Thornton its largest city. Its 2020 population was 519,572.

08003.description: Alamosa is the county seat of Alamosa County, Colorado. The county had 16,376 residents in 2020, and its name is Spanish for a grove of cottonwood trees.

08005.description: This populous Denver-area county includes Aurora, its largest city, while Littleton is the county seat. Arapahoe County had 655,070 residents in 2020.

08007.description: Pagosa Springs is the county seat and only incorporated municipality in this southwestern Colorado county. Its 2020 population was 13,359.

08009.description: At Colorado’s southeastern corner, this county meets Kansas, New Mexico and Oklahoma. Springfield is the county seat; the 2020 population was 3,506.

08011.description: Las Animas is the county seat and only incorporated municipality in this southeastern Colorado county. Its 2020 population was 5,650.

08013.description: Boulder is both the county seat and its most populous municipality, in the Front Range west of Denver. The county’s 2020 population was 330,758.

08014.description: Broomfield is a consolidated city and county midway between Denver and Boulder. Technology growth helped expand its economy in the 1990s; its 2020 population was 74,112.

08015.description: Salida is the county seat of Chaffee County, Colorado, with the Sangre de Cristo Range visible beyond the city. The county had 19,476 residents in 2020.

08017.description: Cheyenne Wells is the county seat of this eastern Colorado county, where numerous creeks and the Smoky Hill River drain the plains. The 2020 population was 1,748.

08019.description: Georgetown is the county seat of Clear Creek County, Colorado. The county had 9,397 residents in 2020, and water covers about 0.3 percent of its total area.

08021.description: Conejos County occupies a broad high mountain valley in south-central Colorado. The county seat is the unincorporated community of Conejos; the 2020 population was 7,461.

08023.description: San Luis is the county seat of this southern Colorado county and the oldest continuously occupied town in the state. The 2020 population was 3,499.

08025.description: Lake Meredith, south of Ordway and Sugar City, is the largest of several lakes in this southeastern Colorado county. Ordway is the county seat; the 2020 population was 5,922.

08027.description: Custer County occupies the rugged Wet Mountain Valley below the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. Westcliffe is the county seat; the 2020 population was 4,704.

08029.description: Delta is both the county seat and the name of this western Colorado county. The 2020 population was 31,196.

08031.description: Denver sits in the South Platte River valley, where the Front Range meets the High Plains. As Colorado’s capital and most populous city, its economy spans government, finance and other services.

08033.description: This county is split into two sections by varied terrain near Colorado’s Utah border, such that ordinary travel between them can require leaving the county. Dove Creek is the county seat; the 2020 population was 2,326.

08035.description: Castle Rock is the county seat of this Denver-area county midway between Denver and Colorado Springs. Its population was 357,978 in the 2020 census.

08037.description: The Eagle River flows through this mountain county, whose elevation rises from the Colorado River to Mount of the Holy Cross. Much of the area is within White River National Forest; Eagle is the county seat and Edwards its largest community.

08039.description: Kiowa is the county seat and Elizabeth the largest town in this Denver-area county. The 2020 population was 26,062.

08041.description: Colorado Springs is the county seat of Colorado’s most populous county, with 730,395 residents in 2020. It is also the center of the county’s metropolitan area.

08043.description: Cañon City is the county seat of this county in south-central Colorado, part of the Pueblo–Cañon City micropolitan area. Its 2020 population was 48,939.

08045.description: Glenwood Springs is the county seat of this western Colorado county, while Rifle is its largest community. The county forms the Rifle–Glenwood Springs micropolitan area.

08047.description: Central City is the county seat of this small Front Range county, which is Colorado’s second-smallest by area. Its 2020 population was 5,808.

08049.description: Hot Sulphur Springs is the county seat of this Colorado county, while Granby is its largest community. The 2020 population was 15,717.

08051.description: Gunnison County occupies the high basin between the Continental Divide and the West Elk Mountains. Gunnison is the county seat, at the confluence of Tomichi Creek and the Gunnison River.

08053.description: This remote county in Colorado’s San Juan Mountains includes multiple fourteeners and one of the country’s largest roadless areas. Lake City is the county seat; the 2020 population was 788.

08055.description: Walsenburg is the county seat of this southern Colorado county, named for the landmark Huerfano Butte. The county had 6,820 residents in the 2020 census.

08057.description: Walden is the county seat and only municipality in this northern Colorado county. The 2020 population was 1,379.

08059.description: Golden is the county seat of this Denver-area county, and Lakewood is its most populous city. The state’s population center fell within the county in 2020.

08061.description: Adobe, Rush, Big Sandy and other creeks drain this eastern Colorado county toward the Arkansas River. Eads is the county seat, and the Great Plains Reservoirs provide irrigation water and recreation.

08063.description: Burlington is the county seat of this eastern Colorado county, which had 7,087 residents in the 2020 census.

08065.description: Leadville is the county seat and only municipality in this high Rocky Mountain county. Mount Elbert, Colorado’s highest natural point, rises within its boundaries.

08067.description: Durango is the county seat of this southwestern Colorado county, which includes the Durango Rock Shelters archaeological site and La Plata Mountains. It forms its own micropolitan area.

08069.description: Fort Collins is both the county seat and most populous city of this county on Colorado’s Front Range. The county’s early agriculture grew through river irrigation and sugar beet cultivation.

08071.description: Trinidad is the county seat of Las Animas County, Colorado’s largest county by area. The county takes its name from an older Spanish name for the Purgatoire River.

08073.description: Hugo is the county seat of this eastern Colorado county, where the Arikaree and Republican rivers drain northern areas and creeks flow south. The 2020 population was 5,675.

08075.description: Sterling is the county seat and center of this northeastern Colorado micropolitan area. The county’s 2020 population was 21,528.

08077.description: Grand Junction is both the county seat and largest municipality in western Colorado’s most populous county. The area is named for its many mesas, including Grand Mesa, the world’s largest flat-topped mountain.

08079.description: Mineral County is among Colorado’s least populous counties, with 865 residents in 2020. Creede is its county seat and only incorporated municipality.

08081.description: Moffat County is Colorado’s second-largest by area, spanning 4,751 square miles. Craig is the county seat and center of its micropolitan area.

08083.description: The county includes Mesa Verde National Park, Canyons of the Ancients and other archaeological sites, with much of its land in tribal or federal ownership. Cortez is the county seat.

08085.description: Montrose is both the county seat and the name of this western Colorado micropolitan area. The 2020 population was 42,679.

08087.description: Fort Morgan is the county seat of this northeastern Colorado micropolitan area. The county had 29,111 residents in the 2020 census.

08089.description: La Junta is the county seat of this southeastern Colorado county. The 2020 population was 18,690.

08091.description: This rugged San Juan Mountains county includes Mount Sneffels, Log Hill Mesa and Pleasant Valley. Ouray is the county seat, while Ridgway is its largest town.

08093.description: Park County includes the South Park basin, the headwaters of the South Platte River and Colorado’s geographic center. Fairplay is the county seat and largest incorporated town; Bailey is the largest settlement.

08095.description: Holyoke is the county seat of this northeastern Colorado county on the Nebraska border. Its 2020 population was 4,530.

08097.description: Aspen is both the county seat and largest city in this mountain county. Castle Peak, one of Colorado’s fourteeners, is its highest point.

08099.description: Lamar is the county seat of this southeastern Colorado county in the lower Arkansas River valley. The 2020 population was 11,999.

08101.description: Pueblo is the county seat and center of this south-central Colorado metropolitan area. The county had 168,162 residents in the 2020 census.

08103.description: The White River flows through this northwestern Colorado county, whose seat is Meeker. The 2020 population was 6,529.

08105.description: The Rio Grande flows through this south-central Colorado county, giving it its name. Del Norte is the county seat; its 2020 population was 11,539.

08107.description: Steamboat Springs is the county seat of this northwestern Colorado micropolitan area, which also includes neighboring Moffat County. Its 2020 population was 24,829.

08109.description: Saguache County is Colorado’s seventh-largest by area, despite its 2020 population of 6,368. Saguache is the county seat.

08111.description: This high-elevation county lies in the heart of the San Juan Mountains and is Colorado’s least populous. Silverton is its only incorporated municipality and county seat.

08113.description: Telluride is the county seat of this southwestern Colorado county, named for the San Miguel River. The 2020 population was 8,072.

08115.description: Julesburg is the county seat of this northeastern Colorado county along the Nebraska border. The 2020 population was 2,404.

08117.description: Summit County’s mountainous terrain ranges from Green Mountain Reservoir to Grays Peak. Breckenridge, at high elevation, is the county seat and center of its micropolitan area.

08119.description: Cripple Creek is the county seat of this Colorado Springs-area county, while Woodland Park is its most populous city. The 2020 population was 24,710.

08121.description: Akron is the county seat of this eastern Colorado county, the least populous county named Washington in the United States. The 2020 population was 4,817.

08123.description: The eastern plains of this large county include the Pawnee Buttes and crop fields. Greeley is the county seat; cattle, grain and sugar beets lead its agricultural production, alongside oil and gas.

08125.description: Wray is the county seat of this northeastern Colorado county, where the Arikaree River exits into Kansas. That river crossing is Colorado’s lowest point.

09001.description: This southwestern Connecticut county anchors the state’s New York metropolitan area, with Bridgeport, Stamford, Norwalk and Danbury among its largest cities. Long Island Sound borders the southern edge; its 2020 population was 957,419.

09003.description: The Connecticut River divides this north-central county, joined by tributaries including the Farmington, Mill and Scantic. Hartford, the state capital, is also its largest city; the county had 899,498 residents in 2020.

09005.description: The Berkshire Mountains and Litchfield Hills define this large, low-density county in northwestern Connecticut. It forms the Torrington micropolitan area and had 185,186 residents in 2020.

09007.description: The terrain is mostly level along the Connecticut River and Atlantic coast, rising to gently rolling uplands inland. The county is part of Greater Hartford and had 164,245 residents in 2020.

09009.description: New Haven and Waterbury are two of Connecticut’s largest cities within this south-central county. Water makes up 29.9 percent of its area; its 2020 population was 864,835.

09011.description: This southeastern Connecticut county has mostly level terrain that rises toward Gates Hill in its northern town of Lebanon. It forms the Norwich–New London metropolitan area and includes reservations of four state-recognized Indigenous tribes.

09013.description: Tolland County includes 13 towns in northeastern Connecticut and is part of the Hartford–East Hartford–Middletown metropolitan area. Its 2020 population was 149,788.

09015.description: This northeastern county forms Connecticut’s Quiet Corner and lies within the Quinebaug and Shetucket Rivers Valley National Heritage Corridor. Snow Hill in Ashford is its highest point; the 2020 population was 116,418.

10001.description: Dover, Delaware’s capital, is the county seat and center of the county’s metropolitan area. Water covers about 26.6 percent of this central Delaware county, which had 181,851 residents in 2020.

10003.description: This northern Delaware county is the state’s most populous, with Wilmington as both its county seat and largest city. Brandywine Creek and the Christina River drain the area, whose eastern edge meets the Delaware River and Bay.

10005.description: The largest county in Delaware by area, Sussex occupies the southern Delmarva Peninsula, with 21.7 percent of its area covered by water. Agriculture—especially poultry production—and coastal tourism are central to its economy; Georgetown is the county seat.

11001.description: Washington, D.C. is a federal district and the capital city of the United States, on the northeast bank of the Potomac River and bordered on three sides by Maryland. The Potomac, Anacostia River and Rock Creek help define its geography; water covers about 10.67 percent of the district.

12001.description: Gainesville is the county seat and home of the University of Florida in this north-central Florida county. Water covers about 9.7 percent of its area; the 2020 population was 278,468.

12003.description: The St. Marys River passes through this county, whose northern edge reaches the Okefenokee Swamp and protected lands. Macclenny is the county seat; prisons, a distribution center and manufacturing are among its employers.

12005.description: Panama City is the county seat and center of this Emerald Coast metropolitan area. The county fronts the Gulf of Mexico in Florida’s northwest Panhandle.

12007.description: Starke is both the county seat and largest city of this north-central Florida county. Florida State Prison lies in an unincorporated part of the county.

12009.description: This Atlantic coastal county includes the Indian River Lagoon and parts of the St. Johns River; water covers 34.8 percent of its area. Titusville is the official county seat, with a second administrative center in Viera.

12011.description: This Miami-area county has low, limestone terrain at the eastern edge of the Florida Platform. Fort Lauderdale is its county seat and largest city; its 2020 population was 1,944,375.

12013.description: The Apalachicola River borders this rural Panhandle county, and the Chipola River runs through it. Blountstown is the county seat; the 2020 population was 13,648.

12015.description: Charlotte Harbor Estuary is a major natural feature of this southwest Florida county, where water covers 20.7 percent of the area. Punta Gorda is the county seat and center of the local metropolitan area.

12017.description: This Nature Coast county includes sparsely settled coastal islands and about one-quarter water. Inverness is the county seat, while Homosassa Springs is the largest community.

12019.description: Clay County lies along the west bank of the St. Johns River, with Black Creek flowing into it and Doctors Lake among its waters. Green Cove Springs is the county seat within the Jacksonville metropolitan area.

12021.description: Florida’s largest county by land area includes much of Big Cypress National Preserve and the northern coastal reach of Everglades National Park. East Naples is the county seat; the area is part of the Naples–Marco Island metropolitan region.

12023.description: Osceola National Forest extends into this north-central Florida county. Lake City is the county seat; government, manufacturing, agriculture and forestry are major parts of the local economy.

12027.description: Arcadia is the county seat of this Florida Heartland county, whose terrain rises from sea level along the Peace River to 96 feet at its highest point. The 2020 population was 33,976.

12029.description: Cross City is the county seat of this Big Bend county in northern Florida. Water covers 18.4 percent of the county’s area.

12031.description: Jacksonville and Duval County share a consolidated government in northeastern Florida. The county’s coastal plain includes some rolling hills, and water covers 17.0 percent of its area.

12033.description: This Panhandle county includes Santa Rosa Island south of Pensacola, which is its county seat and only city. About one-quarter of the county’s area is water.

12035.description: Flagler County has 18 miles of Atlantic coastline, with Bunnell as the county seat and Palm Coast as its largest city. It is linked to both the Daytona Beach and Orlando metropolitan regions.

12037.description: Nearly half of this Gulf Coast county’s area is water, and its rivers include the Carrabelle and Ochlockonee. Apalachicola is the county seat; timber, commercial fishing and tourism have shaped the local economy.

12039.description: This Panhandle county is part of the Tallahassee metropolitan area, with Quincy as its county seat. It is the only majority-Black county in Florida.

12041.description: Trenton is the county seat of Florida’s newest county, formed in 1925. A farmers market on State Road 47 serves the surrounding agricultural area.

12043.description: Fisheating Creek flows into Lake Okeechobee through this Florida Heartland county. Moore Haven is the county seat, and the area forms part of the Clewiston micropolitan region.

12045.description: Port St. Joe is the county seat of this Panhandle county, which is part of the Panama City metropolitan area. Water makes up about one-quarter of its area.

12047.description: This north-central county is separated from other Florida counties by the Suwannee and Withlacoochee rivers, but it touches Georgia by land. Jasper is the county seat; population was 14,004 in 2020.

12049.description: Hardee County lies in Florida’s Bone Valley, which contains much of North America’s phosphate deposits. Wauchula is the county seat and center of its micropolitan area.

12051.description: Hendry County borders Lake Okeechobee, and the Lake Okeechobee Scenic Trail crosses it. LaBelle is the county seat; the county is part of the Clewiston micropolitan area.

12053.description: Brooksville is the county seat and Spring Hill the largest community in this west-central Florida county. The area is part of the Nature Coast and the Tampa metropolitan region.

12055.description: Lake Istokpoga and the Kissimmee River shape this Florida Heartland county’s eastern edge. Sebring is the county seat and center of the local metropolitan area.

12057.description: Tampa Bay borders this west-central Florida county, where unincorporated land makes up most of the county’s area. The county had 1,459,762 residents in 2020; agriculture and cigar-making were historically important.

12059.description: Bonifay is the county seat of this Panhandle county. It is among Florida’s smallest counties by total area and had 19,653 residents in 2020.

12061.description: Vero Beach is the county seat of Indian River County, where water covers about 18.5 percent of the total area. Healthcare, education, government and retail are important employment sectors.

12063.description: Jackson County is the only Florida county that borders both Alabama and Georgia. Marianna is the county seat, and its eastern boundary marks a change between Central and Eastern time zones.

12065.description: This Big Bend county is a narrow land bridge between Georgia and the Gulf of Mexico. Monticello is the county seat; the county is part of the Tallahassee metropolitan area.

12067.description: Mayo is the county seat of this north-central Florida county, the state’s second-least populous in 2020. Its population was 8,226.

12069.description: This central Florida county is named for its many lakes and includes Sugarloaf Mountain, the highest point on peninsular Florida. Tavares is the county seat and Clermont the largest city.

12071.description: Fort Myers is the county seat and Cape Coral the largest city in this Gulf Coast county. The Caloosahatchee and several other rivers cross the area, where construction, retail, leisure and hospitality are major sectors.

12073.description: Tallahassee, Florida’s capital, is the county seat and home to two of the state’s major public universities. Unlike much of Florida, the county has rolling hills in the Red Hills region.

12075.description: Bronson is the county seat of this north-central Florida county, which has been part of the Gainesville metropolitan area since 2018. Water covers 20.9 percent of its area.

12077.description: The Apalachicola River borders this Big Bend county, which also contains Torreya State Park and Apalachicola National Forest. Bristol is the county seat; the 2020 population was 7,974.

12079.description: Madison is the county seat of this Big Bend county in northern Florida. The 2020 population was 17,968.

12081.description: Bradenton is both the county seat and largest city of this county, part of the Sarasota metropolitan area. Its coastline opens to the southern Tampa Bay estuary.

12083.description: Rolling hills, live oaks, pines and palms characterize this North Central Florida county. Ocala is the county seat, and part of Ocala National Forest lies within its boundaries.

12085.description: Stuart is the county seat of this southeastern Florida county, which is part of the Port St. Lucie metropolitan area. Water makes up 27.8 percent of its area.

12086.description: Miami-Dade County is Florida’s most populous county, with 2,701,767 residents in the 2020 census. Biscayne Bay and the Atlantic account for much of its water area; Miami is the county seat and urban center.

12087.description: More than 99.9 percent of Monroe County’s population lives in the Florida Keys, while the mainland portion is largely Everglades National Park. Key West is the county seat; tourism is a major employer.

12089.description: The northeasternmost Florida county ranges from tree farms inland to Amelia Island and Fernandina Beach on the coast. The county seat is Fernandina Beach; forestry and a paper mill are among the major employers.

12091.description: This Panhandle county stretches from Alabama to the Gulf, including rolling wooded hills and Blackwater River State Forest in the north. Military and defense spending are major economic drivers; Crestview is the county seat.

12093.description: Okeechobee County is part of Florida’s Heartland and the Okeechobee micropolitan area. Its 2020 population was 39,644, and Okeechobee is the county seat.

12095.description: Orlando is the county seat and core of this central Florida metropolitan area, which had 1,429,908 county residents in 2020. The county includes numerous lakes and areas of Florida’s coastal lowlands and Central Highlands.

12097.description: Kissimmee is the county seat of this central Florida county, which includes Lake Tohopekaliga. More than half of residents identified as Hispanic in the 2020 census.

12099.description: This southeastern county includes Atlantic shoreline and part of Lake Okeechobee, as well as extensive farmland. West Palm Beach is the county seat and largest city; the central and western areas retain substantial agricultural land.

12101.description: This Nature Coast county lies north of Tampa and west of Orlando, with Dade City as the county seat and Zephyrhills its largest city. Its 2025 population estimate was 682,179.

12103.description: Pinellas forms a peninsula between the Gulf of Mexico and Tampa Bay, with water covering 55.0 percent of its area. Clearwater and St. Petersburg anchor the urban county, which had 959,107 residents in 2020.

12105.description: Bartow is the county seat and Lakeland the largest city in this Central Florida county, which includes part of the Lake Wales Ridge. Flatland interspersed with gently rolling hills accompanies a local economy shaped by phosphate mining, agriculture and tourism.

12107.description: Sinkhole lakes such as Lake Barco and Lake Suggs reflect this county’s limestone geology and the upper Floridan aquifer. Palatka is the county seat, between Jacksonville, Gainesville, St. Augustine and Daytona Beach.

12109.description: St. Augustine is the county seat and largest incorporated city of this northeastern Florida county. Water covers 26.9 percent of its area; the county forms part of the Jacksonville metropolitan region.

12111.description: Port St. Lucie is the largest city and home to most residents in this southeastern Florida county. Fort Pierce is the county seat; water covers 16.9 percent of the county’s area.

12113.description: Milton lies near the geographic center of this Panhandle county, while Navarre is its most populous community. The county is part of the Pensacola metropolitan area.

12115.description: Sarasota County’s Gulf Coast includes barrier islands and beaches, with more than a fifth of the county’s area covered by water. Sarasota is the county seat; North Port is the largest city.

12117.description: Sanford is both the county seat and largest city in this central Florida county between Orange and Volusia counties. It had 470,856 residents in the 2020 census and is part of metropolitan Orlando.

12119.description: Bushnell is the county seat of this central Florida county, while Wildwood and The Villages are its principal cities. Its 2020 population was 129,752.

12121.description: Live Oak is the county seat of this north-central Florida county. Its 2020 population was 43,474, up from 41,551 in 2010.

12123.description: Perry is the county seat of this Big Bend county, where water covers 15.3 percent of the area. Timber-related activity is reflected in its long-running Florida Forest Festival and “Tree Capital of the South” designation.

12125.description: Florida’s smallest county by area is centered on Lake Butler, its county seat. The 2020 population was 16,147.

12127.description: Volusia County lies between the St. Johns River and the Atlantic Ocean, with water accounting for 23.1 percent of its area. The county had 553,543 residents in 2020.

12129.description: Crawfordville is the county seat of this Big Bend county, where nearly all residents live outside municipalities. The 2020 population was 33,764.

12131.description: Walton County stretches from the Alabama line to the Emerald Coast along the Gulf of Mexico. It contains Britton Hill, Florida’s highest natural point; DeFuniak Springs is the county seat.

12133.description: Chipley is the county seat of this northwestern Florida Panhandle county, which is part of the Panama City metropolitan area. The 2020 population was 25,318.

13001.description: Baxley is the county seat of this southern Georgia county, where the Little Satilla and Altamaha river basins meet. The 2020 population was 18,444.

13003.description: Pearson is the county seat of this southeastern Georgia county, most of which lies in the Satilla River basin. Its 2020 population was 8,286.

13005.description: Alma is the county seat of this southeastern Georgia county, where the Satilla and Little Satilla river basins divide the drainage. Water covers about 9.5 percent of the area.

13007.description: The Flint River basin drains the east and west halves of this southwestern Georgia county through separate waterways. Newton is the county seat and only municipality; the 2020 population was 2,876.

13009.description: Milledgeville, developed along the Oconee River, is the county seat of this central Georgia county. Its terrain rises from the fall line to hillier ground in the north.

13011.description: Homer is the county seat of this northeastern Georgia county, entirely within the Broad River sub-basin of the Savannah River system. The 2020 population was 18,035.

13013.description: Winder is the county seat of this Atlanta-area county, wholly within the Upper Oconee River sub-basin. The 2020 population was 83,505.

13015.description: The Etowah River basin drains most of this northwestern Georgia county, while its northeast lies in the Coosawattee basin. Cartersville is the county seat and an expanding Atlanta suburb.

13017.description: Fitzgerald is the county seat of this southern Georgia micropolitan area. The county’s 2020 population was 17,194, and most of its territory drains toward the Lower Ocmulgee River.

13019.description: Nashville is the county seat of this south-central Georgia county, where the Withlacoochee and Alapaha river sub-basins divide the landscape. The 2020 population was 18,160.
